summary: This informational document identifies and describes requirements for use cases related to network resiliency in Segment Routing (SPRING) networks. It looks at what is needed so traffic can keep flowing when failures occur.

eli5.summary: If a road is blocked, travelers need a way around. This lists what trip-planning networks need so traffic keeps moving after a breakdown.

questions: what are the resiliency requirements for segment routing
how does spring handle network failures
subtitle: Recovery from network failures in segment routing networks.

tldr.problem: Networks suffer link and node failures, and applications need fast recovery so traffic keeps flowing. Different operators need different recovery strategies depending on their topology and policies.
tldr.mechanism: Segment Routing (SPRING) can achieve resiliency in multiple ways: with disjoint end-to-end backup paths (path protection), with local repairs at the node nearest the failure, or with operator-controlled repair paths that respect bandwidth or delay constraints.
tldr.outcome: This RFC defines five use cases and their requirements so that operators can choose and combine recovery strategies that suit their networks and services.

facts.label: Path disjointness

today: RFC 8355 is an Informational RFC describing resiliency requirements for Segment Routing. These use cases inform the design of SPRING protocols and implementations deployed in modern networks.

sections.title: Resiliency in Segment Routing
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SPRING) is a forwarding architecture in which packets are routed based on instructions (segments) inserted at the source, rather than hop-by-hop decisions. This document identifies use cases and requirements for protecting traffic when network components fail.

Network failures are inevitable. When a link or router fails, traffic must be rerouted, either by the ingress node (path protection) or by the node nearest the failure (local protection or fast-reroute). The SPRING architecture enables new ways to achieve these strategies quickly—in sub-50 millisecond timescales—and operators need flexibility to choose protection methods that fit their topology and policies.
sections.eli5: When a network route breaks, traffic needs an alternate path. Different networks want different ways to find that path.

sections.title: Path Protection
sections.content:
In path protection, the ingress router (the source) is responsible for failure recovery. The operator configures two disjoint SPRING paths from the source to the destination: a primary path (T1) and a backup path (T2). These paths must be disjoint—they share no links, nodes, or Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs—groups of components that fail together, such as cables in the same duct).

The two paths can be used in three modes: 1+1 protection (both paths carry traffic concurrently so there is no delay on switchover), ECMP/UCMP (traffic is load-balanced across both paths), or 1:1 protection (only the primary path is used; the backup takes over only when the primary fails). When the primary path fails, traffic switches to the backup in a fast-reroute fashion (sub-50 milliseconds). When the primary recovers, the operator can either revert traffic automatically or manually.
sections.eli5: Keep a second complete alternate route ready. If the main route fails, traffic switches to the backup path.

sections.title: Local Protection Techniques
sections.content:
In local protection (or fast-reroute), the node adjacent to a failure detects it and repairs traffic immediately, without waiting for the entire network to converge on a new path. This is faster than path protection because the repair happens locally.

Two management-free approaches are described. In bypass protection, a node creates a repair path that avoids the failed component and rejoins the primary path immediately downstream. For a link failure, the repair path ends at the next hop; for a node failure, it ends at the next-next hop. In shortest-path-based protection, the node computes the shortest path to the final destination while excluding the failed component, then forwards traffic over that alternate route. Both can protect against link, node, or SRLG failures automatically with no operator configuration.
sections.eli5: The node right before a failure detects it and sends traffic around the broken piece, rejoining the original path further down.

sections.title: Managed Protection and Coexistence
sections.content:
Operators may want to override the automatic repair path selection for business or technical reasons—for example, to avoid overloading a link that would absorb the failed link's traffic. Managed local protection allows the operator to explicitly specify the backup path either as constraints (end at the next-hop, minimize delay, avoid a particular SRLG) or as an explicit route. Upon failure, traffic still recovers in sub-50 milliseconds, but over the operator's chosen path.

Finally, different services in the same network may benefit from different protection strategies: flow F1 uses path protection with disjoint paths, flow F2 uses management-free bypass, and flow F3 uses managed protection via a specific path. The SPRING architecture SHOULD support all these techniques coexisting in the same infrastructure, allowing each service to choose its own recovery method.
sections.eli5: Different services can use different backup routes: some use pre-planned alternates, others let the network figure out a path on the fly, others use operator-chosen routes.

sections.title: Loop Avoidance During Convergence
sections.content:
When a failure occurs, each router in the network updates its routing tables at different times. During this convergence period, temporary routing inconsistencies can create micro-loops: packets that loop back on themselves briefly before converging. In traditional networks, these are short-lived, but with sub-50 millisecond fast-reroute, they can cause packet loss.

The RFC requires that the SPRING architecture provide mechanisms to detect and prevent micro-loops during convergence. One approach is to compute paths during the network convergence calculation (SPF computation) that are guaranteed to be loop-free, then use SPRING's packet-steering capability to guide traffic over those paths while the network stabilizes. This allows operators to deploy fast-reroute without losing traffic to transient loops.
sections.eli5: When the network is updating, traffic can briefly loop. SPRING can steer packets on paths that do not loop while updates happen.

items.title: Bypass Protection
items.text: Repair path avoids the failed component and rejoins the primary path immediately downstream.

items.title: Shortest-Path Protection
items.text: Compute the shortest path to the destination while excluding the failed component.

items.title: Managed Protection
items.text: Operator specifies the backup path via constraints or explicit routes.

items.title: Path Protection
items.text: Maintain disjoint primary and backup end-to-end paths from source to destination.
